{{short description|Concept of flexibility in process of conducting a research study}}
'''Researcher degrees of freedom''' is a concept referring to the inherent flexibility involved in the process of designing and conducting a [[scientific experiment]], and in analyzing its results.

==Overview==
The term reflects the fact that researchers can choose between multiple ways of collecting and analyzing data, and these decisions can be made either arbitrarily or because they, unlike other possible choices, produce a positive and [[statistical significance|statistically significant]] result.<ref name="simmons"/>  The researcher degrees of freedom has positives such as affording the ability to look at nature from different angles, allowing new discoveries and hypotheses to be generated.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tukey |first=J.W. |title=Exploratory data analysis Volume 2 |publisher=Pearson |year=1977}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Box |first=George E. P. |date=December 1976 |title=Science and Statistics |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2286841 |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |volume=71 |issue=356 |pages=791–799 |doi=10.2307/2286841|jstor=2286841 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Groot |first1=Adriaan D. de |title=Thought and choice in chess |last2=Groot |first2=Adrianus Dingeman de |date=1978 |publisher=Mouton |isbn=978-90-279-7914-8 |edition=2 |series=Psychological studies |location=The Hague}}</ref> However, researcher degrees of freedom can lead to [[data dredging]] and other questionable research practices where the different interpretations and analyses are taken for granted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wicherts |first1=Jelte M. |last2=Veldkamp |first2=Coosje L. S. |last3=Augusteijn |first3=Hilde E. M. |last4=Bakker |first4=Marjan |last5=van Aert |first5=Robbie C. M. |last6=van Assen |first6=Marcel A. L. M. |date=2016 |title=Degrees of Freedom in Planning, Running, Analyzing, and Reporting Psychological Studies: A Checklist to Avoid p-Hacking |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=7 |pages=1832 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01832 |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=5122713 |pmid=27933012 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Simmons |first1=Joseph P. |last2=Nelson |first2=Leif D. |last3=Simonsohn |first3=Uri |date=2011-10-17 |title=False-Positive Psychology |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0956797611417632 |journal=Psychological Science |volume=22 |issue=11 |pages=1359–1366 |doi=10.1177/0956797611417632 |pmid=22006061 |s2cid=13802986 |issn=0956-7976 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Their widespread use represents an inherent methodological limitation in [[scientific research]], and contributes to an inflated rate of [[false-positive]] findings.<ref name="simmons">{{Cite journal |last1=Simmons |first1=Joseph P. |last2=Nelson |first2=Leif D. |last3=Simonsohn |first3=Uri |date=November 2011 |title=False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant |journal=Psychological Science |language=en |volume=22 |issue=11 |pages=1359–1366 |doi=10.1177/0956797611417632 |pmid=22006061 |s2cid=13802986 |issn=0956-7976|doi-access= }}</ref> They can also lead to overestimated [[effect size]]s.<ref name="wicherts et al.">{{Cite journal |last1=Wicherts |first1=Jelte M. |last2=Veldkamp |first2=Coosje L. S. |last3=Augusteijn |first3=Hilde E. M. |last4=Bakker |first4=Marjan |last5=van Aert |first5=Robbie C. M. |last6=van Assen |first6=Marcel A. L. M. |date=2016-11-25 |title=Degrees of Freedom in Planning, Running, Analyzing, and Reporting Psychological Studies: A Checklist to Avoid p-Hacking |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=7 |pages=1832 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01832 |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=5122713 |pmid=27933012|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Though the concept of researcher degrees of freedom has mainly been discussed in the context of [[psychology]], it can affect any scientific discipline.<ref name="simmons"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Coretta |first1=Stefano |last2=Casillas |first2=Joseph V. |last3=Roessig |first3=Simon |last4=Franke |first4=Michael |last5=Ahn |first5=Byron |last6=Al-Hoorie |first6=Ali H. |last7=Al-Tamimi |first7=Jalal |last8=Alotaibi |first8=Najd E. |last9=AlShakhori |first9=Mohammed K. |last10=Altmiller |first10=Ruth M. |last11=Arantes |first11=Pablo |last12=Athanasopoulou |first12=Angeliki |last13=Baese-Berk |first13=Melissa M. |last14=Bailey |first14=George |last15=Sangma |first15=Cheman Baira A |date=July 2023 |title=Multidimensional Signals and Analytic Flexibility: Estimating Degrees of Freedom in Human-Speech Analyses |journal=Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |article-number=25152459231162567 |doi=10.1177/25152459231162567 |issn=2515-2459|doi-access=free |hdl=2346/95600 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Like [[publication bias]], the existence of researcher degrees of freedom has the potential to lead to an inflated degree of [[funnel plot]] asymmetry.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Carter |first1=Evan C. |last2=McCullough |first2=Michael E. |date=2014-07-30 |title=Publication bias and the limited strength model of self-control: has the evidence for ego depletion been overestimated? |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |volume=5 |pages=823 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00823 |issn=1664-1078 |pmc=4115664 |pmid=25126083|doi-access=free }}</ref> It is also a potential explanation for [[p-hacking]], as researchers have so many degrees of freedom to draw on, especially in the social and behavioral sciences. [[Multiverse analysis]] is a method that helps bring these degrees of freedom to light. Studies with smaller [[sample size]]s are more susceptible to the biasing influence of researcher degrees of freedom.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schweizer |first1=Geoffrey |last2=Furley |first2=Philip |date=March 2016 |title=Reproducible research in sport and exercise psychology: The role of sample sizes |journal=Psychology of Sport and Exercise |language=en |volume=23 |pages=114–122 |doi=10.1016/j.psychsport.2015.11.005}}</ref>

==Examples==
Steegen et al. (2016) showed how, starting from a single raw data set, applying different reasonable data processing decisions can give rise to a multitude of processed data sets (called the data multiverse), often leading to different statistical results.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Steegen|first1=Sara|last2=Tuerlinckx|first2=Francis|last3=Gelman|first3=Andrew|last4=Vanpaemel|first4=Wolf|date=September 2016|title=Increasing Transparency Through a Multiverse Analysis|journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science|language=en-US|volume=11|issue=5|pages=702–712|doi=10.1177/1745691616658637|pmid=27694465|issn=1745-6916|doi-access=free}}</ref> Wicherts et al. (2016) provided a list of 34 degrees of freedom (DFs) researchers have when conducting psychological research. The DFs listed span every stage of the research process, from formulating a [[hypothesis]] to the reporting of results. They include conducting exploratory, hypothesis-free research, which the authors note "...pervades many of the researcher DFs that we describe below in the later phases of the study." Other DFs listed in this paper include the creation of multiple manipulated [[independent variable]]s and the measurement of additional variables that may be selected for analysis later on.<ref name="wicherts et al."/>
